claim: The pectoral fins of ancestral fishes had multiple proximal elements connected to their pectoral girdles.
source: The pectoral fins of ancestral fishes had multiple proximal elements connected to their pectoral girdles.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as background information for the study.

claim: During the fin-to-limb transition, anterior proximal elements were lost and only the most posterior one remained as the humerus.
source: During the fin-to-limb transition, anterior proximal elements were lost and only the most posterior one remained as the humerus.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as background information for the study.

claim: The AP positional values in catshark fin buds are shifted more posteriorly than mouse limb buds.
source: In this study, we examined the pectoral fin development of catshark (Scyliorhinus canicula) and revealed that the AP positional values in fin buds are shifted more posteriorly than mouse limb buds.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by gene expression data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Catshark fins lack a specific AP patterning mechanism which restricts Gli3 expression to an anterior domain in tetrapods.
source: Furthermore, examination of Gli3 function and regulation shows that catshark fins lack a specific AP patterning mechanism, which restricts its expression to an anterior domain in tetrapods.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by Gli3 expression and enhancer analysis data.

claim: Experimental perturbation of AP patterning in catshark fin buds results in an expansion of posterior values and loss of anterior skeletal elements.
source: Finally, experimental perturbation of AP patterning in catshark fin buds results in an expansion of posterior values and loss of anterior skeletal elements.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by RA treatment experiments.

claim: A key genetic event of the fin-to-limb transformation was alteration of the AP patterning network.
source: Together, these results suggest that a key genetic event of the fin-to-limb transformation was alteration of the AP patterning network.
evidence: This is the main conclusion of the study, inferred from the experimental data presented.

claim: Changes in regulatory interactions between transcriptional factors may be key players for patterning changes during morphological evolution.
source: Regulatory interactions between transcriptional factors play important roles for interpreting a morphogen gradient as positional information (Balaskas et al., 2012). Changes in these regulatory interactions may therefore be key players for patterning changes during morphological evolution.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work and serves as the conceptual framework for the study.

claim: Carl Gegenbaur subdivided the skeletal elements of shark pectoral fins into three segments along the AP axis: propterygium, mesopterygium, and metapterygium.
source: 150 years ago Carl Gegenbaur subdivided the skeletal elements of shark pectoral fins into three segments along the anterior–posterior (AP) axis: propterygium, mesopterygium, and metapterygium (Gegenbaur, 1865) (Figure 1A)
evidence: This is a historical fact supported by citation and illustrated in Figure 1A.

claim: Propterygium, mesopterygium, and metapterygium are found in the majority of chondrichthyans, none-teleost actinopterygians, placoderms, and acanthodians.
source: which are also found in the majority of chondrichthyans, none-teleost actinopterygians, placoderms, and acanthodians (Orvig, 1962; Coates, 1994, 2003).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Possession of propterygium, mesopterygium, and metapterygium is considered to be a plesiomorphic state for gnathostomes.
source: Therefore, possession of propterygium, mesopterygium, and metapterygium is considered to be a plesiomorphic state for gnathostomes.
evidence: This is an inference based on the phylogenetic distribution of these structures cited in previous sentences.

claim: In sarcopterygians, the propterygium and mesopterygium have been lost.
source: In the sarcopterygians (lobe-finned fishes including tetrapods), the propterygium and mesopterygium have been lost (Coates, 2003)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: Anterior positional values have been lost or reduced during tetrapod evolution.
source: thus, suggesting that anterior positional values have been lost or reduced during tetrapod evolution.
evidence: This is an inference based on the loss of anterior skeletal elements in sarcopterygians.

claim: In mouse limb buds, Hand2, Gli3, and Shh are key genes for controlling AP patterning.
source: In mouse limb buds, Hand2, Gli3, and Shh are key genes for controlling AP patterning (Riddle et al., 1993; Te Welscher et al., 2002).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: One of the earliest patterning events in mouse limb buds is the mutual transcriptional repression between Gli3 in the anterior tissue and Hand2 in the posterior.
source: One of the earliest patterning events is the mutual transcriptional repression between Gli3 in the anterior tissue and Hand2 in the posterior (Te Welscher et al., 2002; Osterwalder et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Early polarity in Gli3 and Hand2 expression contributes to the subsequent posterior localized expression of Shh.
source: This early polarity in expression contributes to the subsequent posterior localized expression of Shh
evidence: This is based on established knowledge of limb development cited in the manuscript.

claim: Shh reinforces the anteriorly restricted Gli3 protein activity by inhibiting the default processing of the Gli3 protein to its repressor form.
source: and this morphogen in turn reinforces the anteriorly restricted Gli3 protein activity (Shh inhibits the default processing of the Gli3 protein to its repressor form (Gli3R), thus, creating a gradient of Gli3R along the AP axis) (Wang et al., 2000).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: Posterior Shh expression is conserved among gnathostomes.
source: Several studies on fin development of actinopterygians and chondrichthyans have revealed that posterior Shh expression is conserved among gnathostomes (Dahn et al., 2007; Davis et al., 2007; Yonei-Tamura et al., 2008; Sakamoto et al., 2009a).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: In fish fin development, the detailed roles of Shh signalling for AP patterning are not well studied.
source: However, in fish fin development, the detailed roles of Shh signalling for AP patterning are not well studied and the role of the Hand2-Gli3 mutual interaction remains to be elucidated.
evidence: This is a statement about the state of knowledge in the field.

claim: In the mouse limb bud, Alx4, Pax9, Hand1, and Zic3 are positively regulated by Gli3R.
source: In the mouse limb bud, Alx4, Pax9, Hand1, and Zic3 are positively regulated by Gli3R (Te Welscher et al., 2002; Fernandez-Teran et al., 2003; McGlinn et al., 2005; Vokes et al., 2008)
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: In mouse limb buds, Alx4, Pax9, Hand1, and Zic3 are expressed in a localized anterior domain (one-third of the axis).
source: and thus are expressed in a localized anterior domain (one-third of the axis)
evidence: This is based on established knowledge of mouse limb development.

claim: In mouse limb buds, Hand2 and Tbx2 show broad posterior expression domains (two-thirds and one-half of the axis, respectively).
source: while Hand2 and Tbx2 show broad posterior expression domains (two-thirds and one-half of the axis, respectively).
evidence: This is based on established knowledge of mouse limb development.

claim: In stage 30 S. canicula embryos, Alx4 is expressed in half the fin bud.
source: In stage 30 S. canicula embryos (staged according to Ballard et al., 1993), we found instead that the anterior genes Alx4, Pax9, Hand1, and Zic3 were expressed in broad domains, which extend more posteriorly than in the mouse (half the fin bud for Alx4
evidence: This is supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: In stage 30 S. canicula embryos, Pax9 is expressed in two-thirds of the fin bud.
source: two-thirds for Pax9
evidence: This is supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: In stage 30 S. canicula embryos, Hand1 is expressed in two-thirds of the fin bud.
source: two-thirds for Pax9 and Hand1
evidence: This is supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: In stage 30 S. canicula embryos, Zic3 is expressed throughout the whole axis of the fin bud.
source: and the whole axis for Zic3, Figure 1B–E).
evidence: This is supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: In stage 30 S. canicula embryos, the Hand2 and Tbx2 domains are more posteriorly restricted than in mouse limb buds.
source: By contrast, the Hand2 and Tbx2 domains were more posteriorly restricted in S. canicula fin buds than in mouse limb buds (Figure 1F,G).
evidence: This is supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figures 1F and 1G.

claim: All 6 AP patterning genes (Alx4, Pax9, Hand1, Zic3, Hand2, Tbx2) show expression boundaries that are more posterior in S. canicula fin buds than in mouse limb buds.
source: All of these 6 AP patterning genes show the same trend—their expression boundaries are more posterior in S. canicula fin buds (Figure 1H), apparently reflecting a gross shift in the AP coordinate system.
evidence: This is a summary of the gene expression data shown in Figures 1B-G and schematized in Figure 1H.

claim: The posterior shift in AP gene expression boundaries in S. canicula fin buds reflects a gross shift in the AP coordinate system.
source: All of these 6 AP patterning genes show the same trend—their expression boundaries are more posterior in S. canicula fin buds (Figure 1H), apparently reflecting a gross shift in the AP coordinate system.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the gene expression data.

claim: The shifts in AP gene expression boundaries in S. canicula fin buds are observed from stage 29 to stage 31.
source: We chose 3 of these genes to test at multiple time-points to determine whether this was a transient gene expression state (Figure 1—figure supplements 2, 3), but in all cases these shifts were observed from stage 29 to stage 31 (which covers ∼30 days of S. canicula development).
evidence: This is supported by time-course gene expression data shown in Figure 1—figure supplements 2 and 3.

claim: Stage 29 in S. canicula is a stage where Sox9 expression starts in the proximal part of the pectoral fin buds.
source: In particular, stage 29 is a stage where Sox9 expression (a prechondrogenic marker) starts in the proximal part of the pectoral fin buds (Figure 1—figure supplement 2E)
evidence: This is supported by Sox9 expression data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2E.

claim: The observed shift of AP values in S. canicula fin buds would affect proximal skeletal elements as well as distal.
source: which suggest that the observed shift of AP values would affect proximal skeletal elements as well as distal.
evidence: This is an inference based on the timing of Sox9 expression relative to the AP gene expression shifts.

claim: The AP patterning genes Alx4, Pax9, Hand1, Zic3, Hand2, and Tbx2 are regulated by Shh–Gli3 pathway.
source: Since the above AP patterning genes are regulated by Shh–Gli3 pathway (Te Welscher et al., 2002; Fernandez-Teran et al., 2003; McGlinn et al., 2005; Galli et al., 2010)
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: In tetrapod limb buds, Gli3 expression is restricted to the anterior region.
source: In striking contrast to tetrapod limb buds (Büscher et al., 1997; Schweitzer et al., 2000), Gli3 expression is not restricted to the anterior region
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work on tetrapod limb development.

claim: In S. canicula pectoral fin buds, Gli3 expression is not restricted to the anterior region.
source: In striking contrast to tetrapod limb buds (Büscher et al., 1997; Schweitzer et al., 2000), Gli3 expression is not restricted to the anterior region—thus again indicating a general posterior shift of AP positional values in the S. canicula.
evidence: This is supported by Gli3 expression data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: The lack of anterior restriction of Gli3 expression in S. canicula indicates a general posterior shift of AP positional values.
source: In striking contrast to tetrapod limb buds (Büscher et al., 1997; Schweitzer et al., 2000), Gli3 expression is not restricted to the anterior region—thus again indicating a general posterior shift of AP positional values in the S. canicula.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the Gli3 expression data.

claim: Callorhinchus milii has propterygium in its pectoral fin.
source: To address whether this situation is conserved in other chondrichthyans, we also cloned and analysed the expression of Gli3 in pectoral fin buds of a holocephalian, Callorhinchus milii, which has propterygium (Figure 2B)
evidence: This is supported by skeletal staining shown in Figure 2B.

claim: In C. milii pectoral fin buds at stage 31, Gli3 is expressed in the posterior part.
source: and again found expression in the posterior part of pectoral fin bud at stage 31 (staged according to Didier et al., 1998; Figure 2B).
evidence: This is supported by Gli3 expression data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: The overlap of Hand2 and Gli3 expression in chondrichthyans suggests that the Hand2–Gli3 mutual inhibition seen in tetrapods is weak or non-existent in chondrichthyans.
source: Since Hand2 is expressed posteriorly and thus now overlaps with Gli3, this strongly suggests that the Hand2–Gli3 mutual inhibition seen in tetrapods is weak or non-existent in chondrichthyans.
evidence: This is an inference based on the overlapping expression patterns of Hand2 and Gli3 in chondrichthyans.

claim: In chick and mouse limb buds, Gli2 does not play a major role in AP patterning because of its weak processing efficiency to produce its repressor form.
source: In chick and mouse limb buds, Gli2 does not play a major role in AP patterning because of its weak processing efficiency to produce its repressor form (Wang et al., 2000).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: In zebrafish, Gli2 acts as a repressor.
source: However, in zebrafish, Gli2 does indeed act as a repressor (Maurya et al., 2013)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: In S. canicula embryos, Gli2 expression is uniform until stage 29.
source: First, we analysed Gli2 expression in S. canicula embryos and found it to be uniform until stage 29 (Figure 2C)
evidence: This is supported by Gli2 expression data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: In S. canicula embryos after stage 29, Gli2 expression is restricted to the posterior region.
source: and then subsequently restricted to the posterior region (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is supported by Gli2 expression data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: The processing determinant domain (PDD) determines the differential processing efficiencies of Gli3 and Gli2 in mice and humans.
source: We analysed the processing determinant domain (PDD), which determines the differential processing efficiencies of Gli3 and Gli2 in mice and humans (Pan and Wang, 2007).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: Human and S. canicula Gli2 PDD do not induce Gli3R in HEK293 cells treated with forskolin.
source: Human and S. canicula Gli2 PDD did not induce Gli3R, whereas their Gli3 PDDs did (Figure 2E).
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: Human and S. canicula Gli3 PDD induce Gli3R in HEK293 cells treated with forskolin.
source: Human and S. canicula Gli2 PDD did not induce Gli3R, whereas their Gli3 PDDs did (Figure 2E).
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: In S. canicula, Gli3, but not Gli2, plays the major role in repressor production.
source: Thus, in S. canicula (as in chick and mouse), Gli3, but not Gli2, plays the major role in repressor production.
evidence: This is an inference based on the Gli processing assay data.

claim: Element 1586 is a limb-specific Gli3 enhancer that replicates anterior Gli3 expression in mouse limb buds.
source: To compare Gli3 enhancers in chondrichthyans and tetrapods, we used the VISTA enhancer browser (Visel et al., 2007) and found a limb-specific Gli3 enhancer, element 1586, which replicates anterior Gli3 expression in mouse limb buds.
evidence: This is based on data from the VISTA enhancer browser.

claim: Element 1586 is conserved in tetrapods, coelacanth, and chondrichthyans, but not in gar, medaka, and zebrafish.
source: Consistent with the slow evolutionary rate of chondrichthyans and coelacanth (Amemiya et al., 2013; Renz et al., 2013; Venkatesh et al., 2014), element 1586 is conserved in tetrapods, coelacanth, and chondrichthyans, but not in gar, medaka, and zebrafish (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is supported by sequence alignment data shown in Figure 3A and citations about evolutionary rates.

claim: The chick element 1586 drives GFP expression specifically in anterior tissue of chick limb buds and is repressed in the posterior region.
source: As with endogenous Gli3 expression (Büscher et al., 1997), the chick element 1586 drove GFP expression specifically in anterior tissue and was repressed in the posterior region, even though RFP was expressed throughout the buds (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is supported by enhancer assay data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Element 1586 from both S. canicula and C. milii drives GFP expression in chick limb buds, confirming that its general activity is conserved from sharks to tetrapods.
source: The element 1586 from both S. canicula and C. milii also drove GFP expression in the chick limb buds, confirming that its general activity is conserved from sharks to tetrapods.
evidence: This is supported by enhancer assay data shown in Figures 3D and 3E.

claim: Element 1586 from S. canicula and C. milii lacks the specific posterior repression observed in the chick element when tested in chick limb buds.
source: However, in both cases, the specific posterior repression observed in the chick element was absent (Figure 3D,E).
evidence: This is supported by enhancer assay data shown in Figures 3D and 3E.

claim: The differential activity of element 1586 (with tetrapods showing posterior repression, and chondrichthyans not) recapitulates the differences in Gli3 expression within these groups.
source: Thus, the differential activity of this enhancer (with tetrapods showing posterior repression, and chondrichthyans not) recapitulates the differences in Gli3 expression within these groups.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the enhancer assay data.

claim: A specific sequence can exert posterior repression when inserted into the S. canicula enhancer.
source: Furthermore, by recombining S. canicula and chick enhancers, we identified a sequence that can exert the posterior repression when inserted into the S. canicula enhancer (Figure 3F,G and Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by enhancer recombination assay data shown in Figures 3F, 3G, and Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: The sequence that confers posterior repression contains tetrapod or sarcopterygian-specific sequences.
source: This sequence contains tetrapod or sarcopterygian-specific sequences, suggesting that the posterior repressive activity would have been acquired in a stepwise fashion.
evidence: This is based on sequence alignment data shown in Figure 3G.

claim: The posterior repressive activity of element 1586 would have been acquired in a stepwise fashion during evolution.
source: This sequence contains tetrapod or sarcopterygian-specific sequences, suggesting that the posterior repressive activity would have been acquired in a stepwise fashion.
evidence: This is a speculation based on the sequence analysis.

claim: Activation of Shh signalling by RA is conserved among vertebrate limbs/fins.
source: Activation of Shh signalling by RA is known to be conserved among vertebrate limbs/fins (Riddle et al., 1993; Hoffman et al., 2002; Dahn et al., 2007)
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: RA treatment of S. canicula embryos increases and anteriorly expands Ptch1 expression.
source: and as expected, the most reliable Shh target gene, Ptch1 expression (Marigo et al., 1996; Vokes et al., 2008; and see Figure 1—figure supplement 1F for phylogenetic analysis) was increased and expanded anteriorly (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: RA treatment of S. canicula embryos causes Hand2 expression to extend anteriorly.
source: Consistent with this, Hand2 expression also extended anteriorly (Figure 4B)—probably due to inhibition of Gli3 repressor formation by ectopic activation of Shh signalling (as revealed by the extended Ptch1 expression).
evidence: This is supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: RA treatment of S. canicula embryos causes Pax9 expression to be significantly downregulated with only weak expression in the anterior part of the fin buds.
source: On the other hand, Pax9 expression (an anterior marker) was significantly downregulated and showed only weak expression in the anterior part of the fin buds (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: RA treatment of S. canicula embryos does not significantly shift Alx4 expression.
source: The most anterior regions may not be sensitive to this treatment, as expression of Alx4 was not significantly shifted (Figure 4D)
evidence: This is supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: The lack of Alx4 shift after RA treatment may be due to the lack of inhibitory regulation from Hand2 to Gli3 in S. canicula.
source: and this may be due to the lack of inhibitory regulation from Hand2 to Gli3 described above.
evidence: This is an inference based on the earlier finding that Hand2-Gli3 mutual inhibition is weak or absent in chondrichthyans.

claim: In RA-treated S. canicula pectoral fin buds, Hoxa13 expression is weaker than in control, but a shift in its expression domain is not seen.
source: In RA-treated pectoral fin buds, Hoxa13 expression was weaker than in control, but a shift in its expression domain was not seen (Figure 4E)
evidence: This is supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 4E.

claim: The impact of RA treatment in S. canicula fin buds is primarily on AP patterning rather than on PD patterning or a general impact on development.
source: showing that the impact of RA in these experiments is primarily on the AP patterning (the shifts of Ptch1, Hand2, and Pax9, Figure 4A–C), rather than on PD patterning or a general impact on development.
evidence: This is an inference based on the differential effects of RA on AP markers versus PD markers.

claim: In RA-treated S. canicula pectoral fins, the appearance of distinct anterior elements (propterygium and mesopterygium) is lost.
source: Most intriguingly, we examined skeletal patterns of S. canicula pectoral fins in these partially 'posteriorised' fin buds (Figure 4F). Phenotypes varied from mild to severe but in all cases the appearance of distinct anterior elements (propterygium and mesopterygium) was lost.
evidence: This is supported by skeletal staining data shown in Figure 4F.

claim: In mild RA-treated phenotypes, a proximal element anterior to the metapterygium is attached to the pectoral girdle, which may result from a fusion of the proximal parts of propterygium and mesopterygium.
source: In the mild cases, a proximal element anterior to the metapterygium is attached to the pectoral girdle (single asterisk in Figure 4F). This proximal element may result from a fusion of the proximal parts of propterygium and mesopterygium.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the skeletal phenotype data shown in Figure 4F.

claim: In severe RA-treated phenotypes, the pectoral fin has lost the anterior proximal elements.
source: Whereas, the severe cases still have a fused element anterior to the metapterygial axis (double asterisk in Figure 4F), but this element is not directly attached to the pectoral girdle, indicating that the pectoral fin of the severe phenotype has lost the anterior proximal elements.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the skeletal phenotype data shown in Figure 4F.

claim: In RA-treated S. canicula fins, the posterior metapterygium is larger than normal but retains its strong identity as the primary axis from which radial branching is observed.
source: By contrast, the posterior metapterygium itself was larger than normal, but retained its strong identity as the primary axis from which radial branching was observed.
evidence: This is supported by skeletal staining data shown in Figure 4F.

claim: The main cause of the skeletal phenotype in RA-treated S. canicula fins is likely caused by the AP pattern change.
source: Although RA treatment potentially cause non-specific effects, given the clear affect on AP patterning (the shifts of Ptch1, Hand2, and Pax9, Figure 4A–C), while causing no obvious effects on PD patterning, the main cause of the phenotype is likely caused by the AP pattern change.
evidence: This is an inference based on the specificity of the molecular effects of RA treatment.

claim: S. canicula pectoral fin buds have a gross posterior shift in the AP coordinate system compared to mouse limb buds.
source: In the present study, we have found that S. canicula pectoral fin buds have a gross posterior shift in the AP coordinate system compared to mouse limb buds.
evidence: This is a summary of the gene expression findings.

claim: S. canicula and C. milii lack a specific enhancer activity for Gli3 which in tetrapods mediates the posterior repression.
source: We show that S. canicula and C. milii lack a specific enhancer activity for Gli3, which in tetrapods mediates the posterior repression
evidence: This is a summary of the enhancer analysis findings.

claim: The genetic difference in Gli3 enhancer activity likely contributes to the shift of AP positional information in chondrichthyans.
source: and that this genetic difference likely contributes to the shift of AP positional information.
evidence: This is an inference based on the enhancer analysis data.

claim: A partial posteriorisation of S. canicula fin buds leads to a loss of anterior proximal elements (propterygium and mesopterygium).
source: Finally, RA treatment analyses suggest that a partial posteriorisation of S. canicula fin buds leads to a loss of anterior proximal elements (propterygium and mesopterygium).
evidence: This is a summary of the RA treatment findings.

claim: One of the key events during the fin-to-limb transition was an anterior shift of AP positional information (a posteriorisation), which caused the loss of anterior proximal elements.
source: Considering all these data together, we therefore propose that one of the key events during the fin-to-limb transition was an anterior shift of AP positional information (a posteriorisation), which caused the loss of anterior proximal elements (Figure 4G).
evidence: This is the main conclusion of the study, integrating all the findings.

claim: Anterior shift in AP positional information may have had an impact on the distal radials during the fin-to-limb transformation.
source: In the RA treatment experiments, we also observed that the anterior distal radials reduced and only metapterygial radials retained, suggesting that anterior shift in AP positional information may also have had an impact on the distal radials during the fin-to-limb transformation.
evidence: This is a speculation based on the RA treatment phenotype.

claim: The digital arch model proposes that the distal end of the metapterygial axis bent anteriorly during acquisition of digits.
source: Interestingly, nearly 30 years ago, a classic study proposed that the distal end of the metapterygial axis (which has a uniformly posterior position in chondrychthians) bent anteriorly during acquisition of digits—the so-called digital arch model (Shubin and Alberch, 1986; Oster et al., 1988).
evidence: This is a reference to a previous hypothesis in the literature.

claim: There is a possibility that an AP shift in molecular patterning was involved in the acquisition of digits.
source: Although the detailed validity of this model is unclear (Wagner and Larsson, 2007), there is a possibility that an AP shift in molecular patterning was involved in the acquisition of digits.
evidence: This is a speculation connecting the current findings to the digital arch model.

claim: Knockdown of actinotrichia proteins shows an anterior shift in several gene expressions in zebrafish pectoral fin buds.
source: In addition to our RA treatment analysis, knockdown analyses of actinotrichia proteins, which are components of fin rays and lost in tetrapod, show an anterior shift in several gene expressions in zebrafish pectoral fin buds (Zhang et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: AP positional information may have shifted several times until the acquisition of digits.
source: Therefore, it is interesting to speculate that AP positional information may have shifted several times until the acquisition of digits.
evidence: This is a speculation based on the current findings and previous work on actinotrichia.

claim: The Gli3 regulatory region of S. canicula and C. milii lacks the tetrapod-specific repressive element needed for the Gli3–Hand2 interaction in mouse limb buds.
source: We have shown that the Gli3 regulatory region of S. canicula and C. milii lacks the tetrapod-specific repressive element, which is likely needed for the Gli3–Hand2 interaction in mouse limb buds.
evidence: This is a summary of the enhancer analysis findings.

claim: In mice, Gli3−/−; Hand2−/c limbs show a severe dysplastic humerus.
source: In mice, Gli3−/−; Hand2−/c limbs show a severe dysplastic humerus (some of them have ectopic protrusion in humerus; Osterwalder et al., 2014)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: The Gli3–Hand2 interaction has an important role for patterning the proximal elements in mice.
source: suggesting that the Gli3–Hand2 interaction has an important role for patterning the proximal elements.
evidence: This is an inference based on the cited mouse mutant phenotype.

claim: Gli3−/−; Plzf−/− mice lack a femur.
source: For example, Gli3−/−; Plzf−/− mice lack a femur, and Gli3−/−; Alx4−/− mice exhibit humerus malformation (Barna et al., 2005; Panman et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Gli3−/−; Alx4−/− mice exhibit humerus malformation.
source: For example, Gli3−/−; Plzf−/− mice lack a femur, and Gli3−/−; Alx4−/− mice exhibit humerus malformation (Barna et al., 2005; Panman et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Evolutionary modification of Gli3 regulation is likely necessary, but additional regulatory modifications are required for the loss of the anterior elements.
source: These facts suggest that evolutionary modification of Gli3 regulation is likely necessary, but additional regulatory modifications are required for the loss of the anterior elements.
evidence: This is an inference based on the mouse mutant phenotypes.

claim: Changes in morphogen interpretation by gene regulatory network mutations may have a major impact on morphological evolution.
source: In conclusion, by taking advantage of the slow evolutionary rates of chondrichthyian genomes, we were able to precisely compare the gene expression, function and regulation between pectoral fin and limb development, and discover a key difference between them. In particular, our study suggest that changes in morphogen interpretation by gene regulatory network mutations may have a major impact on morphological evolution.
evidence: This is the overarching conclusion of the study.

claim: Ptch1 is the most reliable Shh target gene.
source: and as expected, the most reliable Shh target gene, Ptch1 expression (Marigo et al., 1996; Vokes et al., 2008; and see Figure 1—figure supplement 1F for phylogenetic analysis)
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Hoxa13 is a marker for a late developmental stage in tetrapod limb buds.
source: Hoxa13, which is a marker for a late developmental stage in tetrapod limb buds, was detected since stage 29 in a distal domain.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge of limb development and supported by expression data in Figure 1—figure supplement 2D.

claim: In S. canicula, Hoxa13 is detected since stage 29 in a distal domain.
source: Hoxa13, which is a marker for a late developmental stage in tetrapod limb buds, was detected since stage 29 in a distal domain.
evidence: This is supported by expression data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2D.

claim: Chondrichthyans and coelacanth have slow evolutionary rates.
source: Consistent with the slow evolutionary rate of chondrichthyans and coelacanth (Amemiya et al., 2013; Renz et al., 2013; Venkatesh et al., 2014)
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.
